content.p: In May 1942 Melbourne was living with a wartime brownout, a reduction of street lighting meant to protect the city from air attack, and the streets were crowded with American servicemen. Over roughly two weeks three women were strangled in the city's dark streets and parkland. The killer became known as the Brownout Strangler, a name taken from the brownout. The man police eventually charged was a private born in New Jersey and raised in New York, named Edward Joseph Leonski. He confessed, and he was tried not by an Australian court but by a United States court-martial sitting in Melbourne.
content.h2: A soldier with a troubled record
content.p: Leonski was born on 12 December 1917 in Kenvil, New Jersey, the sixth child of Russian-born parents. The Australian Dictionary of Biography describes a home in which his mother was mentally unstable, two of his brothers had prison records and a third was in a psychiatric hospital. He left junior high school in 1933, completed a secretarial course near the top of his class, and held a series of clerical jobs before working for a food-store chain. He was called up for military service on 17 February 1941.

At San Antonio, Texas, where he was posted to the 52nd Signal Battalion, he began drinking heavily. The Australian Dictionary of Biography says that during this period he once tried to strangle a woman. The army shipped him to Australia, and he reached Melbourne in February 1942, where he was quartered at Camp Pell in Royal Park. The same biography argues that the American authorities did not understand the problem they were sending overseas. In Melbourne his drinking continued. Drunkenness brought thirty days in the stockade, and after his release he went on another binge.

The first victim was Ivy Violet McLeod, 40. Her body was found in the early hours of 3 May 1942 in a doorway beside the Bleak House Hotel in Albert Park. A barman who was walking to work that morning reported seeing an American soldier straighten up in an alcove between two buildings and walk away quickly. The Senior reported that police did not treat robbery as the motive, because McLeod still had her purse. The Australian Dictionary of Biography notes that Melbourne newspapers at once called the crime a "Brownout Crime".

The second victim, according to The Melburnian, was Pauline Thompson, 31. Executed Today describes her as a policeman's wife and the mother of two, and says she met Leonski in a restaurant before they went to a bar together. Her body was found on the steps of a house in Spring Street in central Melbourne, where a night watchman discovered it. The Bendigo Advertiser reported that investigators quickly learned she had been seen in the company of a US soldier on the night she died. The paper said the news made many women who had admired the Americans wary of anyone in an American uniform, while many local men already resented the visitors.

The third victim was Gladys Hosking. The Senior gives her age as 40 and says she had been walking home from her work at the Chemistry Library of Melbourne University. Executed Today gives her age as 41. Her body was found on the edge of Royal Park, close to Camp Pell. The sources differ on the day it was discovered: The Melburnian describes a body found in an air-raid trench on the morning of 18 May, while the Bendigo Advertiser and Executed Today place the discovery on the morning of 19 May. The Australian Dictionary of Biography gives 18 May as the date of the killing.

The Australian Dictionary of Biography notes that all three women were older than the man later accused of killing them, and that although their genitals were exposed, none had been sexually assaulted.

After Hosking's death, several women came forward to say that an American serviceman had attacked them and that they had got away. Oz at War describes one escape in which a person in a hallway distracted the attacker, and another in which the woman's uncle chased the man off. The Melburnian reports that witnesses who had been near the murder scenes, and women who had survived attacks, picked the accused out of a line-up of servicemen. Oz at War, which puts the number of men at Camp Pell at 15,000, says the line-up was held there, and that Leonski was identified by the uncle of a woman who had escaped his attack and by an Australian soldier who had seen a mud-covered American near the park on the night of the third killing.

The Australian Dictionary of Biography gives the arrest date as 22 May 1942 and credits detective work and the testimony of a fellow soldier, to whom Leonski had confided. The State Library of Victoria account adds that Leonski admitted to another soldier that he had killed two women, and that when that soldier urged him to give himself up and plead temporary insanity, he refused. Sources do not agree on the name of the Australian soldier who saw the muddy American near Royal Park. The State Library names Neil Seymour, and Oz at War names Noel Seymour.

When he was arrested, Leonski did not deny the murders. The Senior reports that he confessed and said he had killed the women to "get at their voices." The Australian Dictionary of Biography quotes one statement from him: "I wanted that voice. I choked her." Executed Today reports that in his confession Leonski recalled Thompson singing on their walk home. Executed Today also reports the view of Ivan Chapman, author of an out-of-print 1982 book on Leonski, that forensic methods of the time would not have produced a positive match from his trousers, and that the yellow mud on them could have been picked up elsewhere. On that view the case rested heavily on the confessions.

Leonski's crimes were committed on Australian soil, but he was American, and the Curtin government was careful about its relations with its wartime ally. The Australian Dictionary of Biography says the government decided, after consulting Britain and against some strong opposition, that a United States court-martial could try him. The State Library of Victoria says this was the first time anyone had been tried in Australia by a military tribunal for a crime that broke civilian law. The trial was held in Melbourne, with the case conducted under American military law.

The court found him guilty on 17 July 1942 and sentenced him to death. WW2 Gravestone says his defence attorney, Ira C. Rothgerber, tried to win an external review, without success, and that the case later contributed to the development of the Uniform Code of Military Justice. The Australian Dictionary of Biography says he was declared sane after a dispute about his mental state. The Bendigo Advertiser describes the story as unknown to many Australians and reports that it is the subject of a new book by Ian Shaw, Murder at Dusk. The Oz at War page says that during the proceedings he was cheerful and often took notes.

Evidence at the trial suggested that Leonski might have had two personalities. The State Library of Victoria quotes court testimony that his voice changed when he drank and that at times he seemed to be talking to someone else. It also reports that he had boasted of an alter ego called "Buddy" and claimed that Buddy was the one who committed the crimes. The State Library says the truth behind the murders remains a mystery.

Views from the experts differed. Executed Today reports that the forensic psychiatrist Fredric Wertham, who never met Leonski, believed he was insane and that the murders grew from his relationship with his mother. Army psychiatrists, according to the same article, judged him a psychopath who was not psychotic and who understood that his acts were wrong. The Australian Dictionary of Biography records that the court declared him sane. Ww2gravestone, citing a psychologist who interviewed him during the trial, describes the killings as an expression of resentment toward his mother.

While he waited, Leonski was held in the city watchhouse. The Australian Dictionary of Biography says he corresponded with a woman in Eltham, learned Oscar Wilde's "The Ballad of Reading Gaol", and became a communicant of the Catholic Church. Oz at War says the death sentence was confirmed by General Douglas MacArthur, and gives the confirmation date as 4 November 1942. WW2 Gravestone gives other dates for the review: 14 October for MacArthur's confirmation and 28 October for a board of review's approval, so the sources differ.

Leonski was hanged at Pentridge Prison in Melbourne on 9 November 1942, aged 24. Executed Today says he was only the second United States serviceman to be executed during the Second World War. It adds that the first, James Rowe, had been hanged in Arizona three weeks earlier after being convicted of murdering another soldier. The Senior reports that the Leonski files were among the closed records released by the Public Record Office Victoria in January 2019.

Leonski's body was moved more than once. Oz at War reports that he was first buried in Springvale Cemetery in Melbourne, then, after his remains were recovered in 1945, reinterred at a United States air force cemetery in Ipswich, west of Brisbane. When the American government decided in 1947 to move its dead from Australia, the remains were sent to the United States. The Australian Dictionary of Biography gives his final resting place as a military cemetery in Honolulu, and Oz at War specifies the Schofield Barracks Post Cemetery in Hawaii, where it says he was buried on 14 April 1949.

The case has stayed in public memory. The Australian Dictionary of Biography notes that Albert Tucker painted "Memory of Leonski" in 1943 as part of his Image of Evil series, and that a novel by Andrew Mallon appeared in 1979. A feature film, Death of a Soldier, was released in 1986, according to the same biography and Oz at War. In January 2019 the Public Record Office Victoria opened a range of closed files from 1942, including Leonski's, and The Senior says the records were of interest to historians and family researchers.

The killings also changed how some Melbourne residents saw the American soldiers in their streets. The Bendigo Advertiser, quoting Ian Shaw, describes a honeymoon period in which Australians, especially women, were fond of the Americans, and says that mood turned once Thompson's body was found and it became known she had been with a US soldier.
